A pin must name a fixed tag or a digest, never :latest. The machine's own policy still decides which images may run there. The pins are kept in the console's database; no file changes.
field.host_image_pins.when_to_change: Pin an image when one machine needs another build (a different CPU architecture, or a newer release you have pulled there), or to keep a version you tested. It applies to the next launch on that machine; running engines keep their image.
field.host_image_pins.risks: A pin the machine's policy does not allow makes every launch of that engine on that machine fail its checks. Running engines are not touched, so a wrong pin shows only at the next launch.
field.host_image_pins.example: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1 for vLLM on one machine, while the others keep the default image.

field.image.summary: Which engine image, and so which engine version, to run, chosen among the images the machine allows.
field.image.details: The image is the packaged engine. Its tag is the version, and the version decides which models and settings work. The default is chosen for you. Newer is not always better: a setting that changes the choice should be tested.
field.image.when_to_change: Leave the default unless a model needs a newer or a specific version, as the launch checks will say.
field.image.risks: An image that is not allowed or not present on the machine blocks the launch.
field.image.example: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.23.0 is an image reference with a pinned version.

field.machine_filter.summary: Show only the models on, or reachable from, one machine.
field.machine_filter.details: The library lists models from every machine. This filter narrows it to those that one machine can use: copies on its own disks and storage it shares over the network. Choose 'any' to see everything.
field.machine_filter.when_to_change: Use it when you are choosing a model for a particular machine.
field.machine_filter.risks: A model that is not shown may still exist on another machine. It must be copied to this one before it can run here.
field.machine_filter.example: Filter to the machine that has the free card.

field.model.summary: Which model to load, whose format decides which engines can run it.
field.model.details: Models come from the machine's library: Hugging Face folders, GGUF files, models in an Ollama store, or plain folders. The model must be on the machine you chose. The fit estimate, the settings offered and the checks all depend on the model.
field.model.when_to_change: Pick a model that fits the card with room for conversations. Look at the fit badge.
field.model.risks: A model that is not on the chosen machine blocks the launch.
field.model.example: organisation/model-8B-Instruct in FP8 for a 96 GB card.

field.name.summary: A label for this instance in lists, charts and the chat page.
field.name.details: A name helps you tell instances apart when you run several. It is also part of the container's name. It can be changed later without a restart. If you leave it empty, the model's name is used.
field.name.when_to_change: Use a name that says what the instance is for, such as 'chat-main'.

field.pin.summary: Keep this instance running: the idle timeout never stops it.
field.pin.details: A pinned instance ignores the default and its own timeout. It stays loaded until you stop it or something makes it fail.
field.pin.when_to_change: Pin an engine that other programs depend on all the time.
field.pin.risks: A pinned engine holds its GPU memory around the clock.

field.policy_mode.summary: Whether the console may change anything on this machine: monitor is look-only, manage allows starting and stopping.
field.policy_mode.details: The machine's own administrator sets this in the node policy, and the console cannot override it. In monitor mode you can see GPUs, memory, disks, engines and models, chat with engines and read model files for copies. In manage mode the console can also launch and stop engines and download or copy models, as far as the policy's other switches allow. The mode shows on each machine and decides whether the launch form lets you start anything there.
field.policy_mode.when_to_change: To launch on a machine that shows monitor, ask its administrator to switch it to manage in the policy file.
field.policy_mode.risks: Manage mode lets whoever controls the console start containers on that machine.

field.preset.summary: A ready-made bundle of settings for a goal, such as balanced, max throughput, low latency, long context, tool agent or reasoning.
field.preset.details: Presets set several related values at once so you do not have to know them. Balanced is a safe start. Throughput serves many users. Low latency favours one fast user. Long context makes room for long prompts. Tool agent and reasoning switch on the parsers those models need. You can change any value after choosing a preset.
field.preset.when_to_change: Start with balanced. Pick another when the goal clearly matches.
field.preset.risks: A preset is generic. Check the fit estimate and the warnings, since it does not know your model.
field.preset.example: Choosing 'long context' for a 200-page document summariser.

field.profile.summary: A saved set of settings for a model and an engine, which you can load again, compare and share.
field.profile.details: A profile stores the values of the launch form under a name. You can save one from the form, load it later, see the differences between two profiles, and export or import them as files. Secret values are not stored in a profile.
field.profile.when_to_change: Save a profile when you found settings that work, so that a later launch starts from them.
field.profile.risks: A profile made for one model may not fit another one.
field.profile.example: 'fp8-long' with a long context and an fp8 KV cache.

field.quant.summary: How compressed the model's numbers are: in a search it filters, and for a GGUF repository it picks one file.
field.quant.details: Smaller formats take less memory and are usually faster, with a small loss of quality. The search filter narrows the list to models published in a format such as FP8 or 4-bit. For a GGUF repository you choose one file by its code, for example Q4_K_M. For engines that can quantize while loading, the matching engine setting is a different control.
field.quant.when_to_change: Choose the least compression that fits your memory: FP8 or Q8 first, then 4-bit if you must.
field.quant.risks: The wrong format for the engine blocks the launch.
field.quant.example: Q4_K_M for a GGUF model that must fit a 12 GB card.

field.revision.summary: Which version of the model's repository to use, where 'main' follows the latest.
field.revision.details: Repositories change over time. A branch name follows its latest state. A tag, or a 40-character commit hash, pins one exact state, so that what you tested is what you run.
field.revision.when_to_change: Leave it empty to follow main. Pin a commit when results must be repeatable.
field.revision.risks: Following main means a model can change under you between two downloads.
field.revision.example: A 40-character commit hash copied from the model's page.

field.root.summary: Which model folder on the machine to download into, or to read a model from.
field.root.details: A machine can have several model folders, each with a kind and a yes or no for writing. Downloads and copies can only go to a writable one. The choice also decides which disk the model sits on, and so how fast it loads.
field.root.when_to_change: Pick the folder on the fastest disk with enough free space, or the one your other tools already use.
field.root.risks: A full disk makes the download fail.
field.root.example: A writable folder named 'hf' of kind hf-home on a fast SSD.

field.target_host.summary: The machine that will receive a download or a copy.
field.target_host.details: Files are written into one of that machine's writable model folders. The machine's free disk space decides whether the transfer fits. The machine also checks every file when it arrives.
field.target_host.when_to_change: Choose the machine that will run the model, so the model is local to its GPUs.
field.target_host.risks: A machine that is down, or whose policy forbids writing, cannot receive files.
field.target_host.example: Copy a model to the machine with the free card.

field.ttl.summary: The idle timeout for this instance: how long it may sit without requests before the console stops it.
field.ttl.details: A stopped engine gives its memory back. Starting it again means loading the model again, which can take minutes. Empty uses the console's default. Zero means never stop this one.
field.ttl.when_to_change: Set it for engines you use now and then, so the card is free when you do not need them.
field.ttl.risks: A short timeout stops an engine between a user's questions, and the next one waits for a reload.
field.ttl.example: 30 minutes: the engine is stopped after half an hour without requests.

format.gguf.summary: A single .gguf file, or the first part of a split set, holding weights, tokenizer and settings together.
format.gguf.details: GGUF files come in many quantizations of the same model, each a separate file. The console lists each file with its quantization and size. llama.cpp and Ollama-style engines load this format. Split sets are named like model-00001-of-00003.gguf and are used by pointing at the first part.
format.gguf.when_to_change: Choose a quantization that fits your memory: Q4_K_M is the usual start. Download only the file you need.
format.gguf.risks: A repository with all quantizations is many times larger than one file.
format.gguf.example: A file named model-Q4_K_M.gguf of about 5 GB for an 8-billion-parameter model.

format.hf.summary: A Hugging Face model folder: safetensors weights plus settings files, referred to by its repository ID.
format.hf.details: This is how most open models are published. It lives in a Hugging Face cache folder on the machine and is identified as organisation/name. vLLM, SGLang and other engines that read Hugging Face checkpoints load it. The same model may exist in several revisions, each a snapshot in the cache.
format.hf.when_to_change: Pick this format for vLLM or SGLang. For llama.cpp or Ollama choose a GGUF or Ollama model instead.
format.hf.risks: Choosing an engine that cannot load this format is blocked at preflight.

format.ollama.summary: A model inside an Ollama server's own store, named like llama3:8b.
format.ollama.details: The model is not a file you point at. It lives in the folders (manifests and blobs) that the Ollama server manages, and is referred to by name and tag. The console lists what it finds in the store, and the Ollama engine loads such models by name.
format.ollama.when_to_change: Use this format with the Ollama engine only. To use the same model elsewhere, find its GGUF.
format.ollama.risks: Deleting files by hand inside an Ollama store breaks it. Let Ollama manage the store.

format.other.summary: A folder the console cannot read as a model, which is listed with its size only.
format.other.details: Roots of kind 'other' list one entry per top-level folder, without trying to understand what is inside. Such entries cannot be launched.
format.other.when_to_change: Use it only to see how much space something takes. To run a model, put it in a root whose kind matches.
format.other.example: A folder of datasets next to your models.

format.plain.summary: A model folder with a settings file and weights that sits outside any Hugging Face cache.
format.plain.details: It is the same content as a Hugging Face model, just kept in an ordinary folder, for example converted or fine-tuned on this machine. It is referred to by the folder's location inside a model root rather than by a repository ID.
format.plain.when_to_change: Use it for local or converted models. The console mounts that folder read-only into the engine.
format.plain.risks: A folder without the expected files is not recognised as a model.
format.plain.example: A fine-tuned model saved to a folder under a plain root.

link.connecting.summary: The console is opening a connection to this machine's node.
link.connecting.details: It starts the node (a local process, or over ssh), waits for the node's greeting and checks that both sides speak the same protocol version. On a healthy network this takes a second or two, and it can take up to about half a minute before the console gives up on one attempt.
link.connecting.when_to_change: Wait. If the host keeps switching between connecting and down, read the reason shown for the host.
link.connecting.risks: While a host is connecting, nothing on it can be shown or changed.
link.connecting.example: Right after the console starts, every remote host reads 'connecting' for a moment.

link.disabled.summary: This host is switched off in the host list, so the console does not try to connect to it.
link.disabled.details: The host list has an 'enabled' flag for each machine. When it is false the console keeps the machine listed but opens no connection. The host list is read once, when the console starts.
link.disabled.when_to_change: To use the machine again, set enabled to true in the host list and restart the console.
link.disabled.risks: A disabled host's engines and models are invisible to the console.
link.disabled.example: A machine that is being repaired can be disabled so the console stops retrying.

link.down.summary: The console cannot reach this machine's node, and it keeps trying again, waiting longer each time, up to a minute.
link.down.details: The reason is shown in plain words: the login was refused (the key is not authorised on that machine), the host key is unknown or has changed (check and accept it by hand), the node is not installed, or there is no route to the machine. Problems that need a person are retried only every five minutes. Engines on that machine keep running. The console just cannot see or control them, and it shows the last known model list greyed out.
link.down.when_to_change: Read the reason. Fix it on the machine or in the host list, then press Reconnect to try again straight away.
link.down.risks: Nothing can be launched on a down host. Instances there keep their last known state, so check the machine itself before assuming they are fine.
link.down.example: 'Login refused' after reinstalling a machine means its list of allowed keys lost the hub's key.

link.incompatible.summary: The node and the console speak different versions of their protocol and refuse to work together.
link.incompatible.details: This happens when one side has been updated and the other has not. The message says which side is older. The console retries every five minutes, but a retry only helps after an update.
link.incompatible.when_to_change: Update the older side: usually install the matching node on that machine, or update the console.
link.incompatible.risks: Nothing on this host is shown or controlled until the versions match.
link.incompatible.example: After upgrading the console, a machine that still runs the old node reads 'incompatible'.

link.stale.summary: The connection is open but no fresh measurement has arrived for 6 seconds, so the figures may be old.
link.stale.details: Common causes are a machine that is very busy, a slow network, or a node that is stuck. The figures stay at their last values. The link goes back to up when data resumes. If the silence lasts about 30 seconds, the console drops the link and treats the host as down.
link.stale.when_to_change: Wait a little. If it keeps happening, check the load and the network of that machine.
link.stale.risks: Do not trust numbers on a stale host: they may no longer match reality. Launch checks that depend on free memory use the last known values.
link.stale.example: A host that is swapping heavily may turn stale for several seconds at a time.

link.up.summary: Connected and healthy: the node has said hello and sends a fresh measurement every few seconds.
link.up.details: Everything on this machine can be shown, and, if the machine's policy allows it, managed. The node reports GPUs, memory, disks, containers and models, and the console can talk to engines through it.
link.up.risks: A host that is up but in monitor mode can be watched only. See its mode.
link.up.example: A host is up when its cards, temperatures and instances update every couple of seconds.

management.external.summary: An engine the console found running but did not start, which it can watch but not change unless the machine allows more.
management.external.details: The console recognises engine containers by their image and by how they answer. It reads their state, metrics and models and lets you chat with them when they are reachable. It cannot restart or remove them. Stop and start are offered only when the machine's policy sets external control to stop_start. 'Configure' opens the launch form filled in from the engine's own settings, so you can start a managed copy.
management.external.when_to_change: Leave it alone, or use Configure to create a managed equivalent and then stop the original yourself.
management.external.risks: An external engine sits outside the console's isolation: it may have internet access or other open ports.
management.external.example: A container you started by hand with docker run shows up as external.

management.managed.summary: The console created this engine and has full control: start, stop, restart, remove, logs and settings.
management.managed.details: A managed engine runs in a container the console labelled and started. The console knows its exact settings, shows its logs, and offers every button. It re-attaches to such engines after the console itself restarts. Control is available while the machine is connected and its node is in manage mode.
management.managed.when_to_change: Use managed engines for everything you launch from here.
management.managed.risks: If the machine switches to monitor mode or goes down, the buttons turn off and say why.
management.managed.example: Everything started with the Launch page is managed.

management.script.summary: The machine's operator starts this engine with their own script, and the console can only run that script's actions.
management.script.details: The script is registered in the machine's policy under a name, with actions such as start, stop, status. Start runs the script's start action, stop its stop action, restart both in order. The console never starts or stops the container itself, so rules built into the script, such as 'start the big model before the small one', are always honoured. Settings are decided by the script, not by the console.
management.script.when_to_change: Use the buttons the script offers. To change how the engine runs, change the script on that machine.
management.script.risks: A script action can take a long time and affect other engines. The console asks for confirmation before running the actions the operator marked as needing it.
management.script.example: A script named 'big-model' with actions up, down and status.

mode.manage.summary: This machine's node may also start and stop engines and change models, within its policy.
mode.manage.details: In manage mode the console can launch and stop containers it created, download and copy models into writable folders, and, if the policy allows, pull images, delete models and stop engines it did not create. Each is still limited by the policy's own switches, the allowed images, the writable folders and the port range.
mode.manage.when_to_change: Choose manage mode only after reading what the policy allows. Narrow the allowed images and writable folders first.
mode.manage.risks: Manage mode on a machine with a broad policy gives whoever controls the hub a lot of reach on that machine.
mode.manage.example: A GPU server set to 'manage' with one writable model folder and two allowed images.

mode.monitor.summary: This machine's node may report and watch, but may not change anything: no starting, stopping, writing or deleting.
mode.monitor.details: In monitor mode the console shows GPUs, memory, disks, running containers and models, scans model folders, talks to engines (chat and benchmarks) and reads model files for copies. Nothing on the machine is changed. It is the safe default the installer writes, and also what a node falls back to when its policy file is missing or unsafe.
mode.monitor.when_to_change: To launch engines or manage models there, the machine's administrator edits the policy file and sets the mode to manage. The console cannot do it for them.
mode.monitor.risks: Launching on a monitor-mode machine is blocked at preflight.

page.arena.summary: Put two models side by side on the same prompt, vote for the better answer, and see a ranking.
page.arena.details: The same prompt goes to two engines and their answers appear next to each other. In blind mode the names are hidden until you vote. Votes feed an Elo rating, so over many votes you get a ranking based on your own prompts, not on a public benchmark.
page.arena.when_to_change: Use it to choose between two models or two settings for your own kind of work.
page.arena.risks: A ranking from a handful of votes is noise. It reflects the prompts you tried, not general quality.
page.arena.example: Ten prompts, six votes for model A, three for B, one tie.

page.bench.summary: Run a speed test on an engine and compare results between runs or settings.
page.bench.details: The benchmark sends standard prompts at several levels of concurrency and records prompt speed, answer speed, time to first token, token gap and total time. Results are stored with the settings used, so you can compare two runs or two models fairly.
page.bench.when_to_change: Use it after changing a setting, or to compare models on your hardware. Do not run it on an engine that people are using.
page.bench.risks: It puts real load on the engine. On an engine the console did not start, it asks you to confirm first.
page.bench.example: Compare a run with prefix caching on and one with it off.

page.chat.summary: Talk to a running engine in your browser, with streaming answers, history and adjustable settings.
page.chat.details: Pick an engine that is ready and type. Answers stream in as they are written. You can change the temperature and the token limit, give a system prompt, attach images for models that read them, keep a history and export a conversation. It uses the same path as other clients, so it is a good test that an engine works.
page.chat.when_to_change: Use it to try a model right after launching it.
page.chat.risks: Conversations are stored in the console's own database, on its machine, as plain text.
page.chat.example: Ask a new model to summarise a paragraph and read the speed shown while it writes.

page.config.summary: A safe editor for the console's three configuration files: draft one, check it with the real rules, then install it yourself.
page.config.details:
It covers hosts.json (the hub's machine list), the hub's env file and a machine's node policy. The page never writes a file and runs no command. It can load the current hosts.json, read-only and for admins only, when the console's own loader accepts it. It never shows the env file, which may hold a token, only its path and whether it exists. A node policy lives on its machine, so you start from a template or paste it.

Validate runs the same checks the console uses when it starts, and for a policy a tested copy of the node's rules; messages name fields, never values. Export shows the difference from the current file and offers Copy, Download and the commands to install it.
page.config.when_to_change: Use it before editing any of the three files by hand, to catch a mistake that would stop the console from starting or drop a machine to monitor mode.
page.config.risks: Nothing changes until you install the file. hosts.json and the env file then need a console restart; a policy takes effect on its machine at once and reaches the console after a Reconnect.
page.config.example: Add a machine to hosts.json, press Validate, then copy the install commands.

page.dashboard.summary: The overview of the whole fleet: every machine's GPUs, the running engines, live speed and any alerts.
page.dashboard.details: Each machine has a card with its graphics cards: memory in use, utilization, temperature and power, with small history charts. Each engine has a tile with its state, live tokens per second and how full its KV cache is. A strip at the top lists alerts, such as low RAM, a hot GPU, a failed engine or a machine that is not connected.
page.dashboard.when_to_change: Start here. When something feels slow, the dashboard usually shows which machine or engine to look at next. Click a tile or a card to open it.
page.dashboard.example: A dashboard with one red alert and one engine at 100% KV cache points you to where to look first.

page.discover.summary: Search Hugging Face for models, see their size and whether they would fit, and download them.
page.discover.details: Search by name and filter by task, quantization, size or whether the model is gated. Each result shows a fit badge for your machines and engines, a model card and the files with their sizes. You choose the machine and folder to download to. For GGUF models you pick one quantization, because a repository often holds many.
page.discover.when_to_change: Use it when the model you want is not in the library yet. Check the size against the free disk space first.
page.discover.risks: Large downloads use a lot of bandwidth and disk. A gated model needs a token and an accepted licence.
page.discover.example: Searching 'fp8' and picking the 14 GB version of a model.

page.downloads.summary: Every download and copy, with its progress, speed and time left, and controls to pause, resume or cancel.
page.downloads.details: Downloads from Hugging Face and copies between machines appear in one list. Two run at a time and the others wait in the queue. Each row shows the machine and folder it goes to and the file being transferred.
page.downloads.when_to_change: Open it to follow a long download or to pause one while you need the bandwidth.
page.downloads.example: A 60 GB download at 100 MB/s shows about ten minutes left.

page.host.summary: One machine in detail: its GPUs and who uses them, memory, disks and model folders, images, scripts and policy.
page.host.details: It breaks down the machine's graphics memory by engine, shows RAM and swap with the alerts, lists the disks and the model folders on them with free space, the engine images present, the lifecycle scripts registered for it, and the policy that limits what the console may do there.
page.host.when_to_change: Open it to see who holds a card's memory, to check free disk space before a download, or to read why something is blocked.
page.host.example: The memory view shows one engine holding 82 GiB of a 96 GiB card.

page.hosts.summary: All the machines the console manages or watches, with their connection state and what they hold.
page.hosts.details: Each machine shows whether it is connected, whether it is in monitor or manage mode, its GPUs and memory, how many engines run on it and how many models are on its disks. A machine that is down still shows the last list of models it reported, greyed out.
page.hosts.when_to_change: Use it to check that every machine is connected, to reconnect one, and to see which machines may be used for launching.
page.hosts.example: Three machines listed: two up in manage mode, one down with the reason 'login refused'.

page.instance.summary: One engine in detail: its state, settings, logs, live metrics, memory use and the buttons that apply to it.
page.instance.details: It shows the stage the engine is in, a progress bar while loading, the logs with follow and filter, the memory the engine holds on each card and in host RAM, charts of its speed and queue, and its exact settings. Actions include stop, restart, remove, pin, set the idle timeout, copy as command and open chat.
page.instance.when_to_change: Open it when an engine is slow, failed or stuck loading. The logs and charts are the first things to read.
page.instance.risks: Changing an instance's name, pin or idle timeout does not restart it. Other settings need a restart.
page.instance.example: A failed instance shows the last log lines and the error 'container exited with code 137'.

page.instances.summary: All engine instances on every machine, with their state, model, speed and buttons to start, stop or open them.
page.instances.details: Managed, script and external engines appear together, each with a badge for who controls it. The columns show the machine, the model, the state, uptime and live speed. Buttons appear only where they apply, for example Start on a stopped instance and Stop on a ready one.
page.instances.when_to_change: Use it as the day-to-day list. Open an instance for its logs, settings and charts.
page.instances.risks: Stopping an instance interrupts anyone who is using it.
page.instances.example: Four instances: two ready, one stopped by the idle timeout, one external.

page.launch.summary: The form for starting an engine: pick the machine, model, engine and settings, see the memory fit, and run the checks.
page.launch.details: Choose the machine first, then the model and the engine. Settings are grouped, and presets give you a sensible starting point for a goal. A memory meter shows per card whether the model fits, and updates as you change memory-related settings. The launch checks list anything that would block or endanger the start. You can copy the exact command, and save the settings as a profile.
page.launch.when_to_change: Use it for full control. If you are new to this, turn on beginner mode and use the guided wizard.
page.launch.risks: Wrong settings are caught by the checks before anything is started, but a launch can still fail later, for example when memory is taken by another program.
page.launch.example: Pick a machine, a model, the 'balanced' preset and check that the meter shows green.

page.learn.summary: The glossary: every term the console uses, explained in plain words, with search.
page.learn.details: Each entry says what a word means, why it matters and where to read more. The same entries open from the info buttons next to settings, numbers and states throughout the console.
page.learn.when_to_change: Use it when you meet a word you do not know, or just to learn how inference engines work.
page.learn.example: Search for 'KV' to read about the KV cache.

page.library.summary: Every model stored on any machine, with its copies, sizes, locations and the engines that can run it.
page.library.details: The library is built from each machine's scans. A model with copies on several machines is listed once, with its copies underneath. Storage shared over the network is recognised and counted once. For each copy you see the machine, the folder and drive, whether an engine is using it, and which engines can load its format. From here you can start a launch, copy a model to another machine, or delete a copy where the machine's policy allows it.
page.library.when_to_change: Use it to find where a model is, to see what takes the space on a drive, and to put a model next to the GPU that will run it.
page.library.risks: Deleting a copy frees its space at once. A model that is used by a running engine cannot be deleted.
page.library.example: A 40 GB model with copies on two machines, one of them in use by a running engine.

page.metrics.summary: Charts over time for an engine or a machine: speed, queue, KV cache, waiting time and memory.
page.metrics.details: Pick an engine or a machine and a time range. The charts draw the engine's own figures, such as tokens per second, requests waiting, KV cache use and time to first token, and the machine's RAM, shared memory and swap. Fifteen minutes are kept at full detail, longer ranges are averages by the hour or the day.
page.metrics.when_to_change: Use it to see when a slowdown started, and to compare before and after a change.
page.metrics.example: A queue that grows at the same time as the KV cache hits 100% shows the cause.

page.settings.summary: The console's own settings: Hugging Face token, defaults, engine images, access keys, appearance and the audit log.
page.settings.details: The token's status is shown but never its value. You can set the default idle timeout, default GPUs and which image is used for each engine. You create and revoke access keys with admin or viewer roles, switch between light and dark, turn beginner mode on, and read the log of everything that changed something.
page.settings.when_to_change: Open it to set up a token for gated models, to create keys for other people, and to turn beginner mode on or off.
page.settings.risks: A key is shown once, when you create it. Admin keys can change everything.
page.settings.example: Set the idle timeout to 30 minutes so unused engines stop after half an hour.

page.usage.summary: How much the engines were used: requests and tokens per model and per day, and at what hours.
page.usage.details: The console records each request that goes through its own chat and arena, with its token counts and time. The page sums them by model, by day and by hour, and can export a CSV file.
page.usage.when_to_change: Use it to see which models are actually used before you decide what to keep loaded.
page.usage.risks: It counts only traffic that goes through the console, not clients that talk to an engine directly.
page.usage.example: A model that was loaded all week and used twice.

page.wizard.summary: A guided way to start an engine: model, then machine, then goal, then review, then launch.
page.wizard.details: Each step asks one question and explains the choice. The goal, such as chat, many users, long documents or agents, picks a preset for you. The review shows what will happen and the launch checks. It leads to the same result as the launch form, with fewer decisions.
page.wizard.when_to_change: Use it if you have not run an inference engine before. Switch to the full form when you want to tune.
page.wizard.example: Pick a model, a machine with a free card, 'long documents', and press Launch.

policy.allow_delete.summary: Whether the console may delete model files on this machine.
policy.allow_delete.details: When it is off, the delete button for model copies is disabled and a cancelled download may leave its partial file behind. When it is on, the console can remove a model copy that no running engine is using, inside a writable model folder. It never deletes a whole model root.
policy.allow_delete.when_to_change: Turn it on for machines where you want to manage disk space from the console. Keep it off elsewhere.
policy.allow_delete.risks: With deletes on, a click removes many gigabytes at once. Models can be downloaded again, other files cannot.
policy.allow_delete.example: A model in use by a running engine cannot be deleted, whatever this says.

policy.allow_ipc_host.summary: Whether engines on this machine may share the host's inter-process memory, which multi-GPU engines can need.
policy.allow_ipc_host.details: Engines that split a model over several GPUs use shared memory to coordinate their workers. Sharing the host's own IPC space is the simple way to give them enough; the alternative is a private area with a large size. Sharing is a small step down in isolation from the host.
policy.allow_ipc_host.when_to_change: Leave it on when you use multi-GPU engines. Turn it off if you only run single-GPU engines.
policy.allow_ipc_host.risks: Off with a multi-GPU engine means a private shared-memory area, which must be large enough or start-up fails.
policy.allow_ipc_host.example: true allows ipc: host for a two-GPU engine.

policy.allow_pull.summary: Whether the console may download (pull) engine images onto this machine.
policy.allow_pull.details: When it is off, the images must already be on the machine, put there by its administrator. When it is on, the console may pull only images that match the allowed list. Pulling is a download of many gigabytes from a registry on the internet, so the machine needs that access.
policy.allow_pull.when_to_change: Leave it off on machines without internet access or where you want full control over what is installed.
policy.allow_pull.risks: If it is off and an image is missing, the launch check says to pull it yourself.
policy.allow_pull.example: false: the launch check says 'image is not present: pull it on that machine'.

policy.engine_images.summary: The list of Docker images this machine allows the console to run.
policy.engine_images.details: Each entry is an exact image reference, or a repository followed by :* to allow any tag, or @sha256:* to allow any digest. An image that matches none of them is refused, whatever the console's own settings say. The list is the main brake on what code can run on the GPUs.
policy.engine_images.when_to_change: Keep it short: only the engines you use. Prefer allowing a specific repository over a wildcard.
policy.engine_images.risks: A broad pattern lets anyone who controls the hub run any image of that repository.
policy.engine_images.example: vllm/vllm-openai:* allows every tag of that repository and nothing else.

policy.engine_network.summary: The name of the internal Docker network on this machine where the console places engines.
policy.engine_network.details: Engines are attached only to this network, which has no route to the internet. The console creates it with the internal flag if it is missing, and refuses to use an existing network that is not internal.
policy.engine_network.when_to_change: Leave the default unless the name collides with something on that machine.
policy.engine_network.risks: A network that was created without the internal flag would give engines internet access, so the console refuses it.

policy.error.summary: A problem with the machine's policy file, during which the node runs in monitor mode.
policy.error.details: The node refuses a policy file that is writable by others, not owned by root where that is required, or not valid. It then behaves as if no policy existed: monitor mode, nothing can be changed. The message says what is wrong.
policy.error.when_to_change: Fix the file on that machine, then press Reconnect. The console cannot repair a policy.
policy.error.risks: Until it is fixed, launches and downloads on that machine are blocked.
policy.error.example: A policy file with group-write permission is refused.

policy.external_control.summary: Whether the console may stop and start engines it did not create on this machine: none or stop_start.
policy.external_control.details: With 'none' (the default) external engines are watch-only. With 'stop_start' the console can stop and start them, but only plain containers recognised as engines. It never touches containers that belong to a registered script, and it cannot reconfigure them.
policy.external_control.when_to_change: Leave it at none unless you want to stop a stray engine from the console. Use a script for engines that need ordering rules.
policy.external_control.risks: Stopping an engine somebody else depends on can interrupt their work.
policy.external_control.example: stop_start lets the dashboard stop an engine that was started by hand.

policy.gateway_image.summary: The image the console uses for each engine's loopback gateway on this machine.
policy.gateway_image.details: The gateway is a tiny nginx container that forwards a loopback port to the engine on its internal network. The policy names it exactly, usually pinned by digest, and the console may start only that image as a gateway. If no gateway image is named, engines on this machine cannot be launched.
policy.gateway_image.when_to_change: Set it to a pinned nginx image that is already on the machine.
policy.gateway_image.risks: A gateway image that is not pinned could change underneath you.

policy.max_shm_gib.summary: The largest shared-memory area, in GiB, the console may give one engine container on this machine.
policy.max_shm_gib.details: Multi-GPU engines need a big /dev/shm to coordinate. The console asks for what the engine needs (usually 16 GiB) and the node refuses anything above this limit.
policy.max_shm_gib.when_to_change: Raise it only if an engine reports shared-memory errors and the machine has the RAM.
policy.max_shm_gib.risks: Shared memory is not reclaimable, so a high limit lets one engine take a large share of the machine's RAM.
policy.max_shm_gib.example: 64 allows a container up to 64 GiB of shared memory.

policy.model_roots.summary: The folders where this machine keeps models, each with an ID, a kind and a yes/no for writing.
policy.model_roots.details: The node can read and write only inside these folders. Their kinds say how to read them. Downloads and copies go to writable ones. Read-only roots, such as a shared network folder, can feed engines but not receive files.
policy.model_roots.when_to_change: Add a root when models live on a new disk. Mark a root writable only when the console should store models there.
policy.model_roots.risks: A writable root lets the console fill that disk with downloads.
policy.model_roots.example: A root 'hf' of kind hf-home, writable, and a root 'shared' of kind auto, read-only.

policy.port_range.summary: The range of loopback ports the console may use for engine gateways on this machine.
policy.port_range.details: Each instance gets its own port from this range, for example 18000 to 18099. The console skips ports that are already in use. When the range is full, new launches are blocked with a 'no free port' check.
policy.port_range.when_to_change: Widen it if you run more than a few engines; keep it away from ports other programs use.
policy.port_range.risks: Too narrow a range stops launches. Overlapping other services' ports causes conflicts.

policy.scripts.summary: The start-and-stop scripts the machine's operator registered for the console to run.
policy.scripts.details: Each script has a name, a label, the containers it owns, and actions. Each action is a fixed command line that stays on the machine. The console only sees names and labels, and can pass one argument from a list the operator allowed. Scripts run without a shell and with a minimal environment.
policy.scripts.when_to_change: Register a script when an engine needs ordering or preparation that the console cannot know about.
policy.scripts.risks: A script runs with the rights of the node's account. Review it like any program you run on your machine.
policy.scripts.example: A 'switch model' action that accepts one of two model names.

root.auto.summary: The node works out the kind of this folder itself by looking at what is inside.
root.auto.details: It recognises a Hugging Face home (a hub folder inside), a hub cache (folders named models--...), an Ollama store (manifests), and otherwise treats it as plain model folders and GGUF files. It is the easiest setting when a folder mixes things.
root.auto.when_to_change: Use it when unsure. Set an explicit kind if detection picks the wrong one.
root.auto.risks: A folder with mixed layouts can be read in an unexpected way.
root.auto.example: A shared folder with both GGUF files and model folders.

root.gguf.summary: A folder holding .gguf files anywhere below it, up to six levels deep.
root.gguf.details: Each file is listed as a model, with its quantization read from its name. Split sets (-00001-of-0000N.gguf) are grouped into one entry. It suits llama.cpp style engines.
root.gguf.when_to_change: Use it for a folder where you keep GGUF downloads.
root.gguf.risks: Very large trees are scanned only up to a limit.
root.gguf.example: A folder with Q4_K_M and Q8_0 files of the same model.

root.hf-home.summary: A Hugging Face home folder: models live in a hub folder inside it.
root.hf-home.details: This is the folder that the HF_HOME setting points at. Models are in hub/models--organisation--name with blobs, snapshots and refs. They are read as Hugging Face models (GGUF-only repositories as GGUF).
root.hf-home.when_to_change: Use it for the folder the console downloads Hugging Face models into.
root.hf-home.risks: Pointing it at the wrong level, the hub folder itself, makes the models invisible. Use hf-hub for that.
root.hf-home.example: A folder that has hub/ inside it.

root.hf-hub.summary: A Hugging Face hub cache folder: model folders named models--organisation--name directly inside it.
root.hf-hub.details: The same layout as hf-home, one level down. It is what you get when a program stores its cache without a hub subfolder. Models are read as Hugging Face models.
root.hf-hub.when_to_change: Use it when the folder you have contains the models-- folders directly.
root.hf-hub.risks: Pointing it at a folder with hub/ inside makes models invisible. Use hf-home for that.

root.ollama.summary: An Ollama home or its models folder, holding manifests and blobs.
root.ollama.details: Models are read from the manifests as name:tag, with sizes from their layers. The console reads this store but never rewrites it.
root.ollama.when_to_change: Use it to let the console see what an Ollama server already has.
root.ollama.risks: Do not edit the store by hand.

root.other.summary: Any other folder: one entry per top-level folder, with its size and nothing else.
root.other.details: The node does not try to understand the content, so nothing in it can be launched. It is useful to see how much space something takes.
root.other.when_to_change: Use it only for space accounting.
root.other.example: A backup folder next to the models.

root.plain.summary: A folder of model directories, each with a settings file and weights, up to three levels deep.
root.plain.details: The node looks for folders that hold a config file next to weights and lists each one as a model. They are referred to by their location in the root, not by a repository ID.
root.plain.when_to_change: Use it for converted or fine-tuned models you keep in ordinary folders.
root.plain.risks: Folders without the expected files are skipped.
root.plain.example: A root with one folder per fine-tune.

state.auth_required.summary: An engine found running by the console answered, but it needs an API key, so its metrics and chat are unavailable.
state.auth_required.details: This applies to engines the console did not start. It watches them read-only. The engine replied with an authorisation error (HTTP 401 or 403) to the console's probes, and the console holds no key for engines it does not own, so it can see that the engine exists but not its models or measurements.
state.auth_required.when_to_change: To monitor it, restart that engine without a key, or launch an equivalent through the console. Otherwise leave it: it still shows that something is using the GPU.
state.auth_required.risks: Not a fault. The engine is protecting itself as configured.
state.auth_required.example: An engine started with an API key shows 'auth required' on the dashboard.

state.failed.summary: The engine exited, never became ready, or lost its gateway, and the error and the last log lines are saved.
state.failed.details: Typical causes are running out of GPU memory at start, a setting or a model the engine cannot use, a wrong or missing image, start-up taking longer than the timeout, or the container being killed. An exit code of 137 often means the machine ran out of RAM. The instance keeps its error text and the engine's last log lines.
state.failed.when_to_change: Read the error and the saved log, fix the cause, then press Start again. A message about memory means smaller settings or a smaller model. A message about a setting names the setting.
state.failed.risks: A failed instance still owns its name and port until you start it again or remove it.
state.failed.example: 'container exited with code 137' usually means the host killed the engine for using too much RAM.

state.loading.summary: The engine is loading the model and getting ready: reading weights, compiling, recording CUDA graphs, warming up.
state.loading.details: This is the longest phase. A large model takes minutes to read from disk, and the first start with a new engine or setting also compiles code. The console shows the current step, and a percentage when the engine's log reports one. When the engine's health check answers, the state becomes ready. If it takes longer than the start-up timeout, 30 minutes by default, the instance is marked failed.
state.loading.when_to_change: Wait and watch the log. If the percentage does not move, check how fast the model's drive is and whether the GPU memory is already used by another engine.
state.loading.risks: Loading can still fail with out of memory near its end, when the KV cache is allocated. Slow network storage makes a load long, not wrong.
state.loading.example: A 70 GB model from a fast SSD may load in about a minute. From a gigabit network share it takes ten minutes.

state.ready.summary: The engine answers its health check and can take requests, with the model in GPU memory even when idle.
state.ready.details: Chat, benchmarks and API clients can use it. Its memory stays reserved until you stop it or the idle timeout does. A ready instance can still turn failed later if its container exits or its gateway disappears.
state.ready.when_to_change: Use it. Pin the instance if the idle timeout must never stop it. Stop it to free the GPU for something else.
state.ready.risks: A ready engine holds its GPU memory whether or not anyone is using it.
state.ready.example: Ready with 0 requests running is idle, not broken.

state.starting.summary: The container has been created and the engine program is booting, but it is not loading the model yet.
state.starting.details: The console has asked the machine to start the engine and its loopback gateway. For a short time the engine is only starting its own program. As soon as its log shows loading progress, the state changes to loading.
state.starting.when_to_change: Normally nothing: wait. If it stays here for more than a minute or two with no log output, open the logs.
state.starting.risks: A missing image or a refused setting usually shows up here as a quick failure rather than a long wait.
state.starting.example: A few seconds after you press Start, an instance reads 'starting', then 'loading'.

state.stopped.summary: The engine is not running, so its model is not in GPU memory and its card is free.
state.stopped.details: A stopped instance keeps its settings and its place in the list, but its container is not running. Nothing is loaded and no GPU memory is held. For an engine the console did not start, 'stopped' is also what you see for about half a minute after its container disappears, before it drops off the list. Starting it again loads the model from scratch.
state.stopped.when_to_change: Press Start to launch it again with the same settings. The launch checks run again first. To change settings, open the launch form filled in with this instance's settings. Remove it if you no longer need it.
state.stopped.risks: If something else has taken the GPU memory in the meantime, the next start can fail the memory check.
state.stopped.example: An instance stopped by the idle timeout shows 'stopped'. Start brings it back.

state.stopping.summary: A stop was requested and the container is shutting down, and the GPU memory is freed when it finishes.
state.stopping.details: The console stops the gateway first and then the engine. The engine gets up to 30 seconds to exit cleanly before Docker ends it. Large engines can need most of that time to give the GPU back.
state.stopping.when_to_change: Wait. If the state does not change and the host shows as down or stale, the machine could not be asked; the console keeps the old state instead of guessing.
state.stopping.risks: Starting another engine on the same card before this one has finished can fail the memory check.
state.stopping.example: 'Stopping' for a few seconds after you press Stop is normal.

state.unreachable.summary: An engine's container was found, but the console could not reach it: no port answered.
state.unreachable.details: This applies to engines the console did not start. The console only talks to engines through the machine's loopback address. If the container publishes no port there, or the published ports did not answer the model-list, health or metrics probes, the engine is listed as unreachable. An engine that listens only on its container's private network cannot be monitored.
state.unreachable.when_to_change: Publish the engine's port on the machine's loopback address, or check that it has finished starting. If it is an engine you want managed, launch it through the console instead.
state.unreachable.risks: An unreachable engine may still hold GPU memory. Check the GPU view of the host.
state.unreachable.example: A container started without any port mapping shows 'unreachable'.

verdict.fits.summary: The estimate says the model fits this GPU with room to spare, at most 90% of its memory budget.
verdict.fits.details: The budget is the card's memory times the share you allow the engine to use. 'Fits' means the weights, the KV cache for your context and concurrency, and the working buffers come to at most 90% of that, and also fit in the memory that is free right now. It is an estimate, not a measurement, so a launch can still fail, but it is unlikely.
verdict.fits.when_to_change: Go ahead. If you later raise the context length or the concurrency, look at the verdict again.
verdict.fits.risks: The estimate has not been calibrated against real launches. Treat it as a good guide, not a guarantee.
verdict.fits.example: A 14 GB model with a short context on a 96 GB card fits easily.

verdict.ok.summary: For host RAM: the extra RAM the engine needs is at most 80% of what is available.
verdict.ok.details: The host RAM check is separate from the GPU one. It counts only memory the kernel cannot take back: program memory, shared memory, and buffers for offload. Model files read from disk are not counted, because the kernel drops that cache when it needs the space. 'Ok' means that need is at most 80% of the available RAM.
verdict.ok.example: An engine that needs about 5 GiB of host RAM on a machine with 100 GiB available is ok.

verdict.tight.summary: The estimate says the model fits, but uses 90% to 100% of the budget, leaving little room for a burst.
verdict.tight.details: The numbers add up but with almost nothing to spare. The estimate has not been checked against real launches, and the KV cache grows with traffic, so this is the zone where launches sometimes fail or the engine later runs out of memory.
verdict.tight.when_to_change: Make some room: shorten the context, lower the concurrency, store the KV cache in fp8, or pick a more compressed model. Or accept the risk and watch the first launch.
verdict.tight.risks: Out of memory at start, or later under load when a long prompt arrives.
verdict.tight.example: A verdict of 95% on a card that another engine shares is risky; 95% on a dedicated card may be fine.

verdict.unknown.summary: The console cannot tell whether the model fits because facts it needs are missing, and it does not guess.
verdict.unknown.details: The estimate needs the model's number of layers, attention heads and sizes, and the GPU's free memory. When the model's settings file is missing or unusual, or the machine's memory cannot be read, the verdict is 'unknown' rather than a made-up number. The launch is still allowed, with a warning.
verdict.unknown.when_to_change: Check the weights size on disk against the card's memory yourself. Then launch and watch the first start, or rescan the library so the model's settings are read.
verdict.unknown.risks: An unknown verdict can still end in out of memory.
verdict.unknown.example: A model folder without a config file gives 'unknown'.

verdict.wont_fit.summary: The estimate says the model will not fit: it needs more than the budget, or more than the memory free right now.
verdict.wont_fit.details: Either the total is above the memory budget of the selected GPUs, or it is above what is free at this moment because another engine or program holds memory. The launch is blocked. If stopping a running engine would make room, the console says which one ('fits if you stop ...').
verdict.wont_fit.when_to_change: Choose a smaller or more compressed model, shorten the context, lower the concurrency, add GPUs with tensor parallelism, or stop the engine that holds the memory.
verdict.wont_fit.risks: Launching it by other means ends with an out-of-memory error and a failed instance.
verdict.wont_fit.example: A 140 GB model on one 96 GB card does not fit. In fp8 (about 70 GB) it does.
